content: 1. Certain mutations in HIV can lead to cross-resistance to other antiretroviral drugs, complicating treatment strategies. The International AIDS Society-USA (IAS-USA) maintains an updated list of significant resistance-associated mutations in the reverse transcriptase (RT), protease (PR), integrase, and envelope genes. 2. HIV drug-resistance testing is recommended for all individuals with HIV infection at the time of entry into care, regardless of whether antiretroviral therapy (ART) will be initiated immediately or deferred. If therapy is deferred, repeat testing should be considered at the time of ART initiation. 3. Genotypic resistance testing is the preferred method for guiding therapy in antiretroviral (ARV)-naïve patients. Standard genotypic testing in ARV-naïve individuals involves identifying mutations in the reverse transcriptase (RT) and protease (PR) genes. 4. If there is concern about transmitted resistance to integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs), providers may consider supplementing standard genotypic resistance testing with an INSTI genotype test. 5. Drug-resistance testing should be performed to guide the selection of active drugs when changing ARV regimens in individuals with virologic failure and HIV RNA levels greater than 1,000 copies/mL. For those with HIV RNA levels between 500 and 1,000 copies/mL, testing may be unsuccessful but should still be considered. 6. Resistance testing is also recommended when managing suboptimal viral load reduction or virologic failure. For individuals failing INSTI-based regimens, genotypic testing for INSTI resistance should be performed to determine whether to include a drug from this class in subsequent regimens. 7. Resistance testing in the context of virologic failure should ideally be performed while the individual is still taking the prescribed ARV drugs or within four weeks of discontinuing therapy. If more than four weeks have elapsed since ARV discontinuation, resistance testing may still provide useful information, but previously selected resistance mutations may be missed. 8. Genotypic resistance testing is recommended for patients with suboptimal virologic responses or virologic failure while on firstor second-line regimens. The addition of phenotypic testing to genotypic testing is generally preferred for individuals with known or suspected complex drug-resistance mutation patterns, particularly to protease inhibitors (PIs). 9. Resistance testing is recommended for all pregnant women before initiating ART and for those entering pregnancy with detectable HIV RNA levels while on therapy. This testing helps guide regimen selection to optimize virologic outcomes. 10. The Stanford University HIV Drug Resistance Database provides valuable guidance for interpreting genotypic resistance test results. Various tools are now available to assist providers in interpreting these results. 11. Clinical trials have demonstrated that consultation with specialists in HIV drug resistance improves virologic outcomes. Clinicians are encouraged to seek specialist input to facilitate the interpretation of genotypic test results and the design of optimal new regimens. 12. These assays involve inserting patient-derived HIV gene sequences into a laboratory clone of HIV or generating pseudotyped viruses that express the patient-derived genes of interest. Viral replication is monitored at different drug concentrations, and the drug concentration that inhibits viral replication by 50% (IC50) is calculated. 13. Automated phenotypic assays, which can produce results in 2 to 3 weeks, are commercially available but are more expensive than genotypic assays. Interpretation of phenotypic assay results can be complicated by incomplete information regarding the specific resistance level associated with drug failure, although clinically significant fold-increase cutoffs are now available for some drugs. 14. Both genotypic and phenotypic assays have limitations, including lack of uniform quality assurance testing, high cost, and insensitivity to minor viral species. Drug-resistant viruses that constitute less than 10% to 20% of the circulating viral population may not be detected by commercially available assays. 15. This reversion can occur within 4 to 6 weeks for some drugs. However, re-initiation of the same ARV agents (or those sharing similar resistance pathways) is usually associated with early drug failure, as the virus present at failure is derived from previously archived resistant virus. 16. Resistance testing is most valuable when performed before or within four weeks after discontinuing drugs. Testing done 4 to 6 weeks after drug discontinuation may still detect mutations, but the absence of detectable resistance must be interpreted cautiously when designing subsequent ARV regimens. 17. Transmission of drug-resistant HIV strains is well-documented and associated with suboptimal virologic response to initial ART. The likelihood of acquiring drug-resistant virus is related to the prevalence of drug resistance in HIV-infected individuals engaging in high-risk behaviors in the community. 18. In the United States and Europe, recent studies suggest that the risk of transmitted virus being resistant to at least one ARV drug ranges from 6% to 16%. Up to 8%, but generally less than 5%, of transmitted viruses exhibit resistance to drugs from more than one class. 19. If therapy is initiated in a person with early HIV infection, baseline resistance testing can guide regimen selection to optimize virologic response. Resistance testing in this situation is recommended, with genotypic assays preferred for this purpose. Treatment initiation should not be delayed pending resistance testing results, but the regimen can be modified if warranted once results are available. 20. In the absence of therapy, resistant viruses may decline over time to below the detection limit of standard resistance tests. However, when therapy is eventually initiated, resistant virus may re-emerge, leading to treatment failure.
